title: The argument against Sold a Story that proves why we need it
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman responds to Michael Pershan's blog post arguing that direct instruction is already the norm in American maths classrooms and that teachers avoid evidence-informed explicit teaching because it is hard. Ashman largely accepts the first claim but rejects the second, using his own career as evidence. He describes teaching for thirteen years in London schools without engaging with research, defaulting to explicit teaching while believing he should do something else. Reading Hattie and then Kirschner, Sweller and Clark led him to a better form of explicit teaching with real-time checking of every student and far more review. He argues that most teachers simply never hear about it because their training is often ideologically opposed, so podcasts like Sold a Story serve a real purpose. He closes by giving teachers the benefit of the doubt.
points: Ashman distinguishes default explicit teaching, which many teachers drift into, from evidence-informed explicit teaching that uses cognitive load theory and retrieval.
His personal arc shows that research reading, not training, transformed his practice and gave him permission to teach explicitly.
He disputes Pershan's explanation that explicit teaching is rare because it is too hard, proposing instead that many teachers never learn of it.
He argues teachers who hear of the approach may assume they already do it, which blunts uptake.
He notes the double standard in how his own impressionistic claims are treated compared with Pershan's.
quotes: Without any particularly solid evidence, Pershan asserts that a form of direct instruction is the norm for teaching mathematics in American schools.
I taught what I would now call ‘default explicit teaching’. I would spend ten to twenty minutes explaining and demonstrating at the board while asking a few questions.
The process of reading research changed everything. Explicit teaching was no longer a guilty secret. It aligned with educational psychology.
I did not have to set seatwork where some students would inevitably become stuck. I could check every student’s response in real time. And I could keep them with me for longer.
And as I learned more about retrieval and spaced practice, the proportion of the lesson devoted to review increased from zero up to a quarter or even a third.
It seems reasonable to assume most teachers are not learning about it during training because their lecturers are often ideologically opposed to it.
And when teachers do hear of evidence-informed explicit teaching, there is a chance they map it onto default explicit teaching and think they do that already.
If they choose to ignore this because it’s too much work, that’s on them. But until then, unlike Pershan, I’ll give teachers the benefit of the doubt.
